reading.name: Syria
reading.headline: Syria is in the Severe tier (97/100, 1st riskiest of 203; 1st of 23 in Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan). Among the most dangerous and fragile places in the world.
reading.ground: War, the near-collapse of the state or a deep economic crisis. Daily life and business are heavily disrupted; outside presence is often limited to essential humanitarian, diplomatic or security work.

drivers.label: Political Stability & Violence
drivers.ground: Political violence, unrest and armed conflict: protests that shut roads and shops, attacks, curfews and, at the extreme, war.
drivers.felt_by: Everyone who is there (residents, staff and travellers) and anything with a fixed location.
evidence: deaths in armed conflict (11.07 deaths per 100k)
a high perceived risk of political violence (25.0 WGI score, 0–100)

drivers.label: Governance & Institutions
drivers.ground: Institutions you can't rely on: slow or biased courts, demands for bribes, rules that change without warning, weak protection of property and contracts.
drivers.felt_by: Businesses, investors and NGOs dealing with officials, permits, contracts or courts.
evidence: a difficult regulatory environment (24.3 WGI score, 0–100)

drivers.label: Social & Humanitarian Pressure
drivers.ground: Pressures that can turn into instability: jobless young people, cost-of-living anger and mass displacement.
drivers.felt_by: Communities, employers and governments. These pressures often signal unrest to come.
evidence: youth unemployment (33.1% of youth labour force)

warnings.label: War-level violence (≥1,000 battle deaths in a year, UCDP threshold)
warnings.meaning: Armed conflict is killing people on a scale that counts as war or active conflict. Fighting can move fast, cut roads and supply lines, and spill into neighbouring areas.
warnings.response: Most governments advise against travel to affected areas; organisations limit presence to essential staff with security plans, and insurers treat the area as a war zone.

warnings.label: Mass displacement (≥5% of population displaced)
warnings.meaning: At least one person in twenty has been forced from their home. Needs for shelter, food and health care are large, and neighbouring countries carry heavy pressure.
warnings.response: Humanitarian agencies scale up through UN-led coordination; donors and host governments plan for long-term displacement as well as emergency relief.

warnings.label: Very high youth unemployment (≥25%)
warnings.meaning: A quarter or more of young people who want work can't find it. Youth unemployment is a well-documented driver of protest movements and emigration.
warnings.response: Employers invest in local hiring and training; analysts watch campuses, social media and fuel or food price decisions as protest triggers.

direction: Over the longer run it has risen from 87 in 2015 to 97 now.

business: Use the score to decide where to look closer: compare with peers (Peers tab) and read the drivers before deciding anything.
Raise due-diligence standards: vet partners and owners, enforce anti-bribery compliance, use international arbitration clauses, and consider political-risk insurance.
Plan for disruption: business-continuity and evacuation plans, security for staff and sites, and insurance that covers political violence.
Look after labour and community relations: watch cost-of-living protests and strikes; local hiring and engagement reduce friction.
ngo: About 41.2% of the population is displaced: plan for shelter, protection, food and health needs through UN-led coordination (OCHA, UNHCR). The largest numbers abroad are in Türkiye, Germany and Lebanon.
Access and safety come first: negotiate access, apply humanitarian principles, and keep a security risk-management plan and duty of care for staff.
Expect bureaucratic hurdles and diversion risk: strengthen financial controls, partner vetting and accountability to affected people.
travel: Check your government's official travel advice for Syria before you go. It changes far faster than annual data.
There is active armed conflict: many governments advise against all or non-essential travel to the affected regions.
Higher violence and crime: avoid travelling at night, use trusted transport, keep a low profile and share your itinerary.
Stay away from demonstrations. Protests can turn violent quickly.
research: Start with the drivers: Political Stability & Violence and Governance & Institutions carry the most risk. Explain why.
Put it in context: Syria ranks 1st of 23 in Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan and the Peers tab shows who is close.
Check whether changes are real: governance moves inside the WGI confidence intervals may be noise (Data tab, Governance).
Test the drivers: the What-if simulator shows which indicators would move the score most.
Write it up: the Assessment builder turns this into a structured brief with probabilities.

caveats: Only 59% of the indicators are available for Syria: treat this reading with extra caution.
Scores are relative: they show where a country sits among the others and give no probability of any event.
The data look backwards: governance scores describe last year and conflict data lag by up to two years. Check current news and official travel advice.
This is general, educational guidance. It is not investment, legal or security advice.
